title: Cyclic sort
summary: When values are 1 to n (or 0 to n), each value has a home index. Swap values home, then scan: any index without its own value marks a gap or a repeat.
idea: Value v belongs at index v − 1. Every swap puts one value home for good, so sorting takes O(n) swaps and needs no extra memory.

signals.see: The values are whole numbers in the range 1 to n (or 0 to n), where n is the length.
signals.think: Each value has a home index. Swap it there instead of using a set or sorting.

signals.see: You must find the missing number, or every missing number.
signals.think: After placing values home, every index k without value k + 1 is a missing number.

signals.see: You must find duplicates with O(1) extra space.
signals.think: A duplicate cannot go home because its twin is already there. It ends up sitting in someone else's gap.

signals.see: You need the smallest missing positive, and values outside 1..n can be ignored.
signals.think: Only values 1..n can fill the first n slots. Skip the rest, place the others home, and scan for the first gap.

phrasings: Tickets numbered 1 to n were sold, but some were lost. Which ticket numbers are missing?
Seat numbers 1 to n were assigned, and some seats were booked twice. Which ones?
Find the smallest positive order number that has not been used yet.

picture.title: Every value has a home
picture.alt: On the left, a set of seen values is built and then checked for every number from 1 to n, using O(n) extra space. On the right, each value is swapped to its home index, value v at index v minus 1, and a final scan finds indexes that do not hold their own value.
picture.caption: The array itself becomes the lookup table.

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 12 whole numbers, each from 1 to how many numbers you enter, separated by commas. Repeats are allowed.

oneLiner: while i < n: v not home and its home lacks v → swap, else i++; then scan k for nums[k] ≠ k + 1

exercise.prompt: nums holds n numbers from 1 to n. One number appears twice, so exactly one number is missing. Return [duplicate, missing]. The starter already swaps every value home. Write the scan: the first index k that does not hold k + 1 gives both answers.
hints: After the swaps, every value except the duplicate is home. The duplicate sits in the one slot whose value is missing.
Find the first k with nums[k] != k + 1. Then nums[k] is the duplicate and k + 1 is the missing number.

complexity.why: Each swap puts one value home for good, so there are at most n swaps plus n moves of i. The scan is one more pass. The array is reused, so extra space is O(1).

mistakes: Moving i forward after a swap. The value swapped in has not been placed yet, so stay at i.
Swapping when the home already holds the same value, which loops forever on duplicates. Compare values, not indexes.
Forgetting to skip values outside 1..n, which index past the end of the array.
Using cyclic sort when the values are not tied to the length, such as arbitrary large ids. Use a hash set instead.
Mixing up 0-based and 1-based homes: decide whether v goes to index v or v − 1.

quiz.question: After swapping nums[i] home, why does i stay where it is?
choices: The value that arrived at i has not been placed yet
Because i is always home after a swap
quiz.explain: The swap brings a new value to index i. It needs its own check, so only move on when nums[i] is home or cannot be placed.

quiz.question: Why is cyclic sort O(n) even though there is a swap loop inside the scan?
choices: Each swap places one value home for good, so there are at most n swaps
It only works on short arrays
It never swaps more than once per index
quiz.explain: A value that is home is never moved again. With n values there can be at most n swaps in total.

quiz.question: nums has n values but some are negative or larger than n. You want the smallest missing positive. What do you do with those values?
choices: Leave them where they are and move on
quiz.explain: Only values 1..n can fill the first n slots. Others are skipped. They end up in gaps, which the scan reports.

interviewTip: Point out the range constraint early: “values are 1 to n, so each one has a home index”. It explains why you can beat the hash-set answer on space.
